title: Setting Up a Nanny Cam: Placement Tips and Best Practices
excerpt: Where should a nanny cam point? Covers sightlines, lighting, power, Wi-Fi reach, the two-minute view test, disclosure, and off-limits rooms.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
A nanny cam earns its keep only if it shows you what actually happened, and placement decides that before any setting does. Point it carelessly and you get a wall, a window glare, or a hallway that never sees the room. This guide covers where to place the camera, how to test the view in minutes, and the habits that make footage worth reviewing.

Skip the impulse to hide the camera first and aim it later. Start with the job: confirming a caregiver arrived, watching a child's play area, seeing meal preparation, or documenting an entry. Each goal points at a different spot, and a camera asked to cover everything usually covers nothing.

Placement spots that work

Elevated corners beat hidden nooks. A high shelf at the corner of a room gives the widest useful view with the fewest blind spots. Entry-adjacent spots — a console near the front door, a bookshelf facing the hallway — capture arrivals without watching private rooms. In playrooms, set the camera at roughly adult eye height or above, angled slightly down, so faces are visible rather than the tops of heads.

The two-minute view test

Before you leave the house, run the test: open live view on your phone, stand in the spots where care actually happens, and check that faces are recognizable. Then check the blind corners. If a person could stand in the room and never enter the frame, the placement fails. Adjust the angle or height and retest — two minutes now saves weeks of useless footage later.

Angles and lighting mistakes that ruin clips

Never point a camera directly at a window. Daylight blows out the image and the room behind becomes a silhouette; at night, passing headlights do the same. Avoid aiming across the room at mirrors or televisions, which bounce light and create glare. Aim along the room's long axis when possible, with the main light source behind the camera, so faces are lit rather than shadowed. Ceiling-down angles work in play areas; avoid aiming up at adults from low furniture, which captures chins and ceilings instead of faces.

Power and battery planning for full-day coverage

A camera that dies at mid-afternoon records nothing of the afternoon. Wired units remove the problem entirely if an outlet is near the spot. Battery units suit rentals and shelf placement, but check the charge before long coverage days and set low-battery alerts in the app. Solar panels and trickle chargers extend runtime on sunny porches; indoors, plan a charging rotation so a spare is always ready.

Wi-Fi reach decides placement more than the camera does

A strong signal is a placement decision. Walk the room with the camera's signal indicator or your phone's Wi-Fi meter before mounting. If the signal is weak where you want the camera, move it closer to the router, add a mesh node, or pick a different spot — a camera struggling to hold a connection drops frames exactly when you need them. Test at the same time of day you will rely on it, since congestion changes through the day.

Before the caregiver arrives

Once placement is set, do three things: confirm recording works end to end (live view, clip saved, notification received), clean the lens, and decide what you will tell the caregiver. Disclosure is a legal question, not just a manners question. Rules on recording in your own home with or without notice vary by state, and audio recording is often treated more strictly than video. Check your local rules before the first shift — our nanny cam legality guide covers the general framework.

What to tell the caregiver

A simple script works: "There is a camera in the living room for everyone's safety. It records video only. The feed is viewable by me and my partner." Stating it plainly sets expectations, avoids surprises, and keeps both the relationship and the recording on firmer ground.

Where a nanny cam must never go

Bathrooms, bedrooms, changing areas, and any space where a child or caregiver expects privacy are off-limits, full stop. Keep cameras out of those rooms regardless of consent, and angle entry and play-area cameras so private spaces stay out of frame. Then review placement monthly: furniture moves, and last month's perfect angle can become this month's view of a wall.

For hiding spots that still capture the room, see 15 spots that work indoors and out, and for general room planning, the home placement guide.
